cues.text: Section five: total cost of ownership and return on investment.
Total cost of ownership, or TCO, includes acquisition, implementation, integration, operation, maintenance, training, security, migration and retirement costs across a defined period.
When you compare alternatives, you must compare them over equivalent scope and equivalent time horizons, otherwise the comparison is not fair.
Now let us look at a table that shows a three-year cost comparison between an on-premises option and a cloud option.
I will go row by row.
First row, initial investment.
On-premises requires thirty million naira, while cloud requires five million naira.
Second row, annual operating cost multiplied by three years.
On-premises comes to eighteen million naira, while cloud comes to thirty million naira.
Third row, migration and exit costs.
On-premises is four million naira, and cloud is five million naira.
Final row, the total.
On-premises totals fifty-two million naira, and cloud totals forty million naira.
Notice the relationship here.
The on-premises option costs much more up front, but its running costs are lower.
The cloud option reverses that pattern: a small initial investment, but higher operating cost over the three years.
In this example, the lower upfront cost of cloud outweighs its higher operating cost, so cloud has the lower total.
However, this is a simplified comparison.
It excludes discounting and residual value.
Also, cloud is cheaper in this example, not universally.
In a real decision you should also consider reliability, data sovereignty, latency, skills and vendor dependency.
Next, return on investment, or ROI.
The formula is: ROI equals total benefits minus total costs, divided by total costs, multiplied by one hundred percent.
For example, if benefits are sixty million naira and costs are forty million naira, then the net gain is twenty million naira, and dividing by forty million gives an ROI of fifty percent.
Benefits can include revenue, cost savings and avoided losses.
But you must avoid double-counting, and you must distinguish estimated benefits from realised benefits.
Finally, cost-benefit analysis compares expected costs and expected benefits.
Keep the three measures distinct.
TCO measures cost.
ROI measures relative net return.
NPV, or net present value, measures discounted net value.
And remember that a low-cost option can be poor value if it cannot meet business needs.
